BRIEF FACTS:
2. It is stated that on 07.10.2017, Sh. S.P. Singh, the Food Safety Officer alongwith other officials visited the shop no. 135 of Sh. Vinod Kumar S/o Late Sh. Trilok Chand Aggarwal at Kucha Ghasi Ram, Chandni Chowk, Delhi6,

and purchased the sample o f " S w e e t A m l a C a n d y " f o r a n a l y s i s u n d e r t h e p r o v i s i o n s o f F S S Act/Rules/Regulations, for which credit note of Rs. 140/ dated 07.10.2017 was given.
The sealed sample packets along with a copy of memo in Form VI were sent to the Food Analyst, Delhi and also to the Designated Officer.
An opportunity was given to the appellant/Food Business Operator (FBO) for sending the fourth packet for analysis to NABL accredited Laboratory under Section 47(1)(c)(3) and 2.4.5 of the rule.

The Food Analyst analyzed the sample and reported the sample to be misbranded because there was violation of Regulation no. 2.2.1.3 read with 2.3.1.5,
2.2.2.1 & 2.2.2.10 of the FSS (P&L) Regulation vide its Report dated 12.10.2017.
The Food Analyst further opined the label of the said article to be misleading as the FSSAI Logo and License Number, list of ingredients and Best Before declaration are not declared on the label.

3. Thereafter, the appellant was provided an opportunity to file an appeal u/s 46(4) of FSS Act within the stipulated period of 30 days, but, no appeal was preferred by the appellants against the report of the Food Analyst.
During the course of hearing before the Ld. Adjudicating Officer, appellants herein have submitted their reply on 29.10.2018 denying the charges leveled against them by the FSO.
Appellants have stated that the sample commodity is Ayurvedic Proprietary Medicine and their product is not misbranded.

The FSO in his counter reply dated 19.12.2018 submitted that Amla Candy is a standardized food article "Candied Fruit" under Regulation No.
2.3.26.1.1 of the Food Safety & Standards (Food Product Standards & Food Additives)
Regulation, 2011 and as such, same is covered under FSS Act/Rules/Regulations.

The impugned order is further assailed on the grounds that sanction given by the Designated Officer is bad in law and there was no proper application of mind and consideration of facts by consenting authority; the Adjudicating Officer did not conduct the fair enquiry in a legal way; no departmental witness or other witnesses were examined and that mandatory requirements of the Act have not been complied with.
8. On filing of the appeal, notice was ordered to be issued to the respondent and although no reply has been filed, the present appeal is vehemently opposed.

DECISION:
9.
I have given my anxious consideration to the submissions made by Sh. R.D. Goel, Ld. Counsel for the appellants and Sh. Vinod Kumar Sharma, Ld. Chief PP for the State/respondent.
I have gone through the record of the Adjudicating Officer and record of the present appeal and documents filed therewith.

10. The opinion dated 12.10.2017 of the Food Analyst, Deptt. of Food Safety, Govt. of NCT of Delhi,
is as follows :
"The sample is misbranded because there is violation of Regulation no. 2.2.1.3 read with 2.3.1.5, 2.2.2.1 & 2.2.2.10 of The Food Safety & Standards (Packaging &
Labelling) Regulation, 2011."

sentences.text: 12 . The sole contention raised on behalf of appellants is that there is no standard of Sweet Amla Candy under Food Safety Act as it is an ayurvedic product, hence, the order of the Adjudicating Officer is not sustainable.
In support of his submission, Ld. Counsel for appellants has relied upon the observation made by the Apex Court in Jagdish Chandra v State of UP (Supra).

entities.text: Jagdish Chandra v State of UP
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In this case, the appellant was convicted of a charge that he sold 450 grams of Dalchini for Rs.2.25 to Food Inspector.
Even the Food Inspector has admitted that he did not know the distinction between Dalchini proper and ChiniDalchini so called.
The court has observed that the sample was not subjected to any chemical test or analytical process, the opinion of the Public Analyst was not entitled to any weight whatsoever.

It further revealed that on the date when sample was examined,
there was no standard prescribed for ChiniDalchini and the standard was prescribed for Chini Dalchini (Cassisa lignea) by the government notification w.e.f. 01.07.1979 only.
It was on this ground the appeal was accepted.
Counsel for the appellants has further relied upon M.V. Krishna Nambissa v State of Kerala (Supra), where the court has observed that standard of one cannot apply to another.

entities.text: M.V. Krishna Nambissa v State of Kerala
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 14. Coming back to the facts of the present case, the FSO had purchased a packet of Sweet Amla Candy on 07.10.2017 from FBO/appellants.
The sealed sample was sent to Food Analyst who has reported the same to be misbranded.

Sections 23,26 & 27 of FSS Act prescribes the Packaging and labelling of foods, Responsibilities of the FBO and liability of Manufacturers, packers, wholesalers,
distributors and sellers.

15. Section 3(1)(zf)(A)(i)(a) of the FSS Act provides that misbranded food means an article of food if it is purported, or is represented to be, or is being offered or promoted for sale with false, misleading or deceptive claims either.

It further provides that if the article contained in the package - contains any artificial flavouring, colouring or chemical preservative and the package is without a declaratory label stating that fact or is not labelled in accordance with the requirements of this Act or regulations made thereunder or is in contravention thereof, the same also means misbranded food.

16. Chapter 2 of The Food Safety and Standards (Packaging and Labelling) Regulations, 2011,
provides the standards of packaging and labelling of food articles.

entities.text: Food Safety and Standards (Packaging and Labelling) Regulations, 2011
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: Regulation No. 2.2.1.3 of the FSS (P&L) Regulation provides that pre packaged food shall not be described or presented on any label or in any labelling manner that is false, misleading or deceptive or is likely to create an erroneous impression regarding its character in any respect.

Further, Regulation No. 2.2.1.5 & 2.2.1.7 of the FSS (P&L) Regulation provides as under :
"5. Contents on the label shall be clear, prominent, indelible and readily legible by the consumer under normal conditions of purcahse and use.
7. Licence number shall be displayed on the principal display panel in the following format, namely :-

sentences.text: Regulation No. 2.2.2.10 of the FSS (P&L) Regulation provides that every package of food shall carry the information mentioning "Best Before and Use By Date".

18. Admittedly by the appellants various requirements of the Regulations of labelling and packaging were not complied with, the sole plea of the appellants is that their product is an Ayurvedic Medicine and these standards provided in the Regulations are not applicable to their product.

On the other hand, the plea of the respondent is that the product of the appellants is standardized food article ("Candied Fruit") under Regulation 2.3.26.1.1 of the Food Safety & Standards (Food Product Standards & Food Additives) Regulation, 2011.

entities.text: Food Safety & Standards (Food Product Standards & Food Additives) Regulation, 2011
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: 19. Regulation 2.3.26.1.1 provides that Candied Fruits/ Vegetables/Rhizome/Fruit Peel means the product prepared from sound and ripe fruits, vegetables, rhizomes or fruit peel, of any suitable variety, appropriately prepared, by impregnating it with nutritive sweeteners to a concentration adequate to preserve it.

20. As already discussed, the sole contention raised on behalf of the appellants is that the sample seized by the FSO from appellants was not subjected to any chemical test or analytical process,
hence, the opinion of the Food Analyst is not of any importance.
It is apparent from the report of the Food Analyst that the product was not subjected to any chemical test or analytical process to give any final conclusion.

These rules and regulations are framed and designed in the manner not only to see that the product with best quality should reach to the public but also with the objective that the manufacturers, sellers or food brand operator should not make such claim which may be deceptive to the customers.
As per the appellants, their product is an Ayurvedic proprietary medicines and same is beyond the purview of these rules and regulations.
If the product of the appellants does not fall in the category of Candied Fruit, primarily this was the responsibility of the appellants to prove.
The case of the appellants is also silent if they have taken authorisation from any appropriate authority to prove their products as "Ayurvedic proprietary medicines".

From the various facts,
discussed in above paras, it stand established that the product of the appellants seized by the FSO falls in the category of "Candied Fruit" as provided under Regulation 2.3.26.1.1 of the Food Safety &
Standards (Food Product Standards & Food Additives) Regulation, 2011.

The same is accordingly dismissed.
